name: Workflow Patterns
question: Do I need an agent at all?
summary: Workflows run the model along code paths you wrote in advance; agents let the model choose its own steps and tools. The three core workflow patterns are prompt chaining (fixed steps with checks between them), routing (classify, then send each input down a specialised path) and parallelization (sectioning or voting). Start with the simplest pattern that works and add agentic freedom only when it measurably helps.
useCases: The steps can be written down before the task starts
Requests fall into a few known types, each with its own procedure
Audit, cost or latency limits call for predictable behaviour

items.detail: a fixed sequence of calls, with plain-code gates between steps
a classifier sends each input to a specialised prompt or path
independent subtasks run at the same time, then join
the same check run several times or with several prompts; aggregate
low-confidence routes go to a general path or a human
the model picks the steps: more flexible, costlier, errors can compound

steps: Write the procedure down and mark which steps need a model at all
Put a plain-code check between steps so bad output stops early
Add a router only when request types need genuinely different handling
Measure accuracy, cost and unhandled cases before reaching for an agent
pitfalls: A router without a fallback silently misroutes unfamiliar requests
Rigid chains break on open-ended tasks nobody anticipated
Voting multiplies cost, so use it only where errors are expensive
remember: Write the path down if you can. Let the model steer only where you can’t.

steps.title: Chain fixed steps
steps.text: The claim email goes through a fixed sequence: a small model extracts the fields, then a path prompt writes the summary. Your code, not the model, decides the order.

steps.title: Gate between steps
steps.text: A plain-code check sits between the steps. A claim with no policy number or amount is sent back for documents instead of producing a confident but wrong summary.

steps.title: Route by request type
steps.text: A cheap classifier sends each claim down a specialised path: cashless 55%, reimbursement 30%, other 15%. Each path has its own prompt and checks.

steps.title: Fall back when unsure
steps.text: If the router's confidence is below 0.7, the claim goes to a general path or a human queue. Without this, unfamiliar requests are silently misrouted.

steps.title: Section: run independent parts together
steps.text: The fraud screen and the summary do not depend on each other, so they run at the same time. The slower one sets the latency: 4.1 s instead of 7.8 s one after the other.

steps.title: Vote where errors are expensive
steps.text: Three independent fraud prompts review the claim and it is flagged when two agree. Voting triples the cost of that check, so keep it for decisions where a miss is costly.

pros: Predictable cost, latency and behaviour: easy to test and audit
Each step can use the cheapest model that passes it
Plain-code gates stop bad inputs before they spread
No framework needed; any engineer can read the code
cons: Breaks on requests nobody designed a path for
Every new request type needs a new path and tests
Routers misroute unless you add a fallback
Voting and extra checks add cost per request
avoidWhen: The steps depend on what the tools return and cannot be listed in advance (use a ReAct loop)
Most requests are open-ended and would all fall through to a general path

playgroundGuide.scenario: A general insurer's health-claims desk handles 1,000 claim emails. You build the pipeline from workflow parts: a router with cheap specialised paths, a completeness gate, a fraud screen that can run in parallel with the summary, and voting on the fraud check. Then switch the task mix to open-ended work and see where a fixed workflow stops coping.

Drag the slider to set the router's confidence threshold; below it, claims go to the general large-model path.
Switch the task mix between predictable and open-ended, or load a scenario.

outputs.name: Accuracy
outputs.meaning: Share of claims handled correctly, including incomplete claims sent back and fraud caught.

outputs.name: Cost vs one generic prompt
outputs.meaning: Cost per 1,000 claims as a share of one large-model prompt plus fraud screen (₹650).

outputs.name: Unhandled tasks
outputs.meaning: Claims that fit no designed path and were sent down a wrong one.

outputs.name: p95 latency
outputs.meaning: Time within which 95% of claims finish; the slow path and the fraud screen set it.

outputs.name: Model calls per claim
outputs.meaning: Average number of model calls for one claim.

outputs.name: To general path · misrouted
outputs.meaning: Share sent to the general large-model path, and share sent down the wrong specialised path.

presets.name: One generic prompt
presets.expect: Every claim goes to the large model: accuracy 71.8%, ₹650 per 1,000 claims, p95 7.5 s.

presets.name: Router + gate
presets.expect: Specialised small-model paths and a gate: accuracy 90.3%, ₹237 per 1,000, but p95 8.3 s.

presets.name: Router + gate + sectioning
presets.expect: The fraud screen runs alongside the summary: same 90.3% and ₹237, p95 down to 5.3 s.

presets.name: Open-ended mix
presets.expect: 35% of tasks fit no path: accuracy falls to 72.1% and 19.3% of tasks are unhandled.

missions.text: Get the cost under ₹400 per 1,000 claims with accuracy at or above 90%.
missions.hint: Switch on the router and the gate. The gate alone is worth 8 points of accuracy.

missions.text: Get p95 latency under 6 s using sectioning, with accuracy still at or above 90%.
missions.hint: With the router and gate on, tick sectioning: the fraud screen no longer waits for the summary.

missions.text: On the open-ended mix with the router on, find where unhandled tasks exceed 20%, the signal that an agent may be warranted.
missions.hint: Lower the confidence threshold to 0.65 or below: fewer unfamiliar tasks fall back to the general path.

tools.best: Chains, routers and parallel calls written as ordinary functions, with nothing between you and the model.
tools.ex: A claims router in 60 lines: a Haiku classifier, three path prompts and a thread pool for the fraud screen.
pros: Nothing to learn beyond the SDK
Every step is visible and testable
cons: Retries, state and tracing are yours to add

tools.best: Workflows as explicit graphs with state, conditional edges and parallel branches, plus persistence.
tools.ex: A graph with a router node, three path subgraphs and a fraud node that runs in parallel with the summary.
pros: Branches and parallel nodes are first-class
Checkpointing and human review built in
cons: Easy to over-engineer a simple chain

tools.best: Small agents with handoffs and guardrails when a step needs a little autonomy inside a mostly fixed flow.
tools.ex: A triage agent hands off to a cashless or reimbursement agent, with an input guardrail for missing policy numbers.
pros: Handoffs and guardrails are built in
cons: Oriented to agents rather than fixed pipelines
Best with OpenAI models, though others work

tools.best: Building agents on the harness behind Claude Code when a path needs tools, files and a loop.
tools.ex: A reimbursement path that reads uploaded bills with file tools while the rest of the pipeline stays fixed.
pros: Tools, permissions and context management included
cons: Heavier than a few API calls for simple chains

tools.best: Durable workflows that survive crashes and retries, for long-running or multi-day processes.
tools.ex: A claim workflow that waits two days for a hospital document, then resumes at the right step.
pros: Retries, timers and state survive failures
cons: A platform to run and learn

practice.scenario: An Indian general insurer's health-claims desk receives about 4,000 emails a day. A cheap classifier routes each one to a cashless, reimbursement or general path; each path is a short chain with a plain-code gate that stops claims with a missing policy number or discharge summary. A fraud screen runs in parallel with the summary, so the team gets predictable cost and an audit trail without an agent deciding anything.

industries.use: Route claims by type, then run fixed extraction and summary chains with completeness gates
Classify service requests (address change, card block, statement) into fixed procedures
Route returns, refunds and delivery queries to specialised prompts, with a human fallback

practice.analogy: A hospital reception desk. The receptionist does not treat anyone; they send each patient to the right department, where a set procedure runs.

library.name: Anthropic Python SDK (plain code)
library.what: Workflows need no framework: a few model calls, ordinary if-statements and a thread pool cover chaining, routing and sectioning.

practice.note: Minimal sketch. Prompts are shortened; add retries, logging and your own schemas before production.

samples.code:
import json
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
SMALL, LARGE = "claude-haiku-4-5", "claude-sonnet-4-5"   # use your current models
PATHS = {"cashless": "Check pre-authorisation fields...",
         "reimbursement": "Check bills, discharge summary...",
         "general": "Answer the policyholder's question..."}

def ask(model, prompt, max_tokens=800):
    r = client.messages.create(model=model, max_tokens=max_tokens,
                               messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
    return r.content[0].text

def route(email):                                   # routing
    out = json.loads(ask(SMALL, 'Classify as cashless, reimbursement or general. '
                                'Reply as JSON {"route": ..., "confidence": 0-1}\n' + email, 100))
    return out["route"] if out["confidence"] >= 0.7 else "general"   # fallback

def handle(email):
    path = route(email)
    fields = json.loads(ask(SMALL, "Extract policy_no, amount, hospital as JSON:\n" + email))
    if not fields.get("policy_no"):                 # gate between chain steps
        return {"status": "sent back", "reason": "policy number missing"}
    with ThreadPoolExecutor() as pool:              # sectioning: run in parallel
        fraud = pool.submit(ask, SMALL, "List fraud red flags:\n" + json.dumps(fields))
        summary = pool.submit(ask, LARGE, PATHS[path] + "\n" + json.dumps(fields))
    return {"route": path, "summary": summary.result(), "flags": fraud.result()}

numericDrill.question: One generic prompt costs ₹0.60 per claim on the large model. The routed design makes a small router call (₹0.03) for every claim, then runs a 2-call small-model chain (₹0.03 per call) for 70% of claims and one large-model call (₹0.60) for the other 30%. What does the routed design cost per 1,000 claims, in ₹?
numericDrill.answer: Router: 1,000 × ₹0.03 = ₹30. Small chains: 700 × 2 × ₹0.03 = ₹42. Large path: 300 × ₹0.60 = ₹180. Total ₹252, against ₹600 for one generic prompt on the large model.

interview.question: When would you choose a workflow over an agent?
interview.answer: When the steps can be written down in advance and requests fall into known types. A workflow is cheaper, faster, easier to test and easier to audit. Move to an agent only for the slice of work where the path depends on what the tools return, and measure that the extra freedom actually improves results.

interview.question: What is the difference between sectioning and voting?
interview.answer: Both are parallelization. Sectioning splits a task into independent parts that run at the same time, such as a fraud screen alongside a summary. Voting runs the same check several times or with several prompts and aggregates the answers, trading extra cost for fewer mistakes.

mistakes.mistake: Building a router with no fallback for low-confidence or unknown requests
mistakes.fix: Send low-confidence routes to a general path or a human, and count them

mistakes.mistake: Reaching for an agent framework before measuring a simple chain
mistakes.fix: Build the simplest chain first and add agentic steps only where metrics show a gap

quiz.question: A health insurer’s claims emails fall into three types, each with a written procedure. The team is choosing between an autonomous agent and fixed code paths. What should it build first?
options: An autonomous agent with every claims tool
A router that sends each type down its own fixed chain
One long prompt listing all three procedures
A tree search over possible procedures
quiz.explanation: The steps are known in advance and the request types are few, so routing to fixed chains is cheaper, faster and easier to audit than an agent.

quiz.question: A bank’s router sends 4% of service requests to the wrong chain, and those customers get irrelevant replies. The misroutes are all low-confidence predictions. What is the most direct fix?
options: Add a confidence threshold with a general or human fallback
Replace the router with a larger model everywhere
Add voting to every chain
Remove the router and use one prompt
quiz.explanation: Low-confidence predictions are where misroutes cluster, so a threshold that falls back to a general path or a human removes most of them.

quiz.question: A returns workflow extracts order details, then drafts a refund note. 6% of emails have no order number, and the drafts for them invent one. What stops this?
options: A larger drafting model
A plain-code gate that checks the order number before drafting
Asking the drafting prompt to be careful
Running the draft step twice
quiz.explanation: A gate between chain steps is cheap and certain: stop and ask for the order number instead of letting a model guess.

quiz.question: One generic prompt costs ₹0.60 per claim. A router call costs ₹0.03; 70% of claims then take a 2-call small chain at ₹0.03 per call and 30% take the ₹0.60 prompt. What is the routed cost per 1,000 claims?
quiz.explanation: Router ₹30, small chains 700 × 2 × ₹0.03 = ₹42, large path 300 × ₹0.60 = ₹180. Total ₹252.

quiz.question: A hospital’s discharge workflow runs a medication check (3.0 s) and a summary (4.5 s) one after the other. Neither needs the other’s output. With sectioning, what is the latency of these two steps?
quiz.explanation: Run in parallel, the slower step sets the time: 4.5 s instead of 3.0 + 4.5 = 7.5 s.

quiz.question: Which of these are workflow patterns rather than agent behaviours? Select all that apply.
options: Prompt chaining with checks between steps
Routing each input to a specialised prompt
The model choosing which tool to call next from what it just saw
Running the same check three times and voting
quiz.explanation: Chaining, routing and parallelization (including voting) follow code paths you wrote. Choosing the next tool from an observation is agent behaviour.

quiz.question: A broker’s support desk sees 20 request types, but 3 of them make up 85% of volume and have fixed procedures. The rest are varied. What design fits?
options: An agent for everything
Workflows for the top 3 types and an agent or human path for the rest
One workflow per request type, all 20
A single generic prompt
quiz.explanation: Fix the predictable bulk with workflows and send the varied tail to a more flexible path; building 20 rigid chains costs more than it saves.

quiz.question: A fraud check is voted on by three independent prompts, and a transaction is flagged when two agree. Each prompt costs ₹0.04. What does voting add per 1,000 transactions compared with one prompt?
quiz.explanation: Three prompts cost ₹0.12 against ₹0.04 for one, so voting adds ₹0.08 × 1,000 = ₹80.

quiz.question: A telecom’s workflow handles SIM, billing and roaming requests well, but open-ended complaints now make up 30% of traffic and 22% of all tasks end up misrouted. Which conclusions are reasonable? Select all that apply.
options: The fixed paths do not cover a large slice of the work
An agent or human path may be warranted for that slice
Adding voting to every chain will solve it
The router should be removed entirely
quiz.explanation: Unhandled tasks above about a fifth signal that fixed paths no longer fit; a more flexible path for that slice is the fix. Voting and removing the router do not address coverage.

quiz.question: A contract-review pipeline extracts clauses, classifies each and then summarises risks. A junior engineer wants to replace it with an agent “to make it smarter”. Accuracy and cost are already on target. What should the team do?
options: Replace it; agents are more capable
Keep the workflow and add an agent only for a measured gap
Add a tree search on top
Double the number of chain steps
quiz.explanation: Add agentic complexity only when it measurably helps. A workflow that meets its targets is cheaper and easier to audit.

quiz.question: A routing prompt classifies requests with probabilities. The code reads: if probs[route] > 0.7: route = "general". What is the effect?
options: Confident predictions go to the general path and unsure ones stay routed
Unsure predictions go to the general path
All requests go to the general path
The router never falls back
quiz.explanation: The comparison is inverted: confident predictions fall back and unsure ones are routed. It should be < 0.7.

quiz.question: An EdTech platform grades essays with one call per essay. For high-stakes final exams it wants fewer grading errors and accepts higher cost. Which pattern fits?
options: Sectioning
Voting across several independent grading prompts
Routing by essay length
A completeness gate
quiz.explanation: Voting runs the same task several times and aggregates, trading cost for fewer errors, which suits high-stakes decisions.

quiz.question: A shipment-exception workflow has a router with a 0.9 confidence threshold. Accuracy is high but costs doubled. Which are likely causes? Select all that apply.
options: Many confident-enough requests now fall back to the expensive general path
The threshold is set too high for this traffic
The gate between steps is too cheap
Sectioning is running steps in parallel
quiz.explanation: A very high threshold sends many routable requests to the general path, which costs more. Lowering it trades a little accuracy for large savings; gates and sectioning do not raise cost.

quiz.question: A lab-report workflow routes 60% of reports to a small-model chain at ₹0.10 and 40% to a large-model path at ₹0.50, plus a ₹0.02 router call on every report. What is the average cost per report?
A loan-application workflow calls a large model to check whether the PAN field is filled in. What is the best change?
options: Replace that step with a plain-code check
Use a larger model for more accuracy
Vote across three models
Move it to the end of the chain
quiz.explanation: Only use a model where one is needed. A field-presence check is ordinary code: free, instant and exact.

quiz.question: A SaaS support team measures its new routed workflow. Which metrics tell it whether routing is working? Select all that apply.
options: Accuracy per route
Share of requests sent to the fallback path
Share of requests that fit no path and were misrouted
Average prompt length per route
quiz.explanation: Per-route accuracy, fallback share and unhandled share show whether paths fit the traffic. Prompt length says nothing about quality.

quiz.question: A claims chain has three steps with success rates of 98%, 95% and 97%, and the steps fail independently. What share of claims pass all three?
options: About 90.3%
About 95.0%
About 93.1%
About 97.0%
quiz.explanation: 0.98 × 0.95 × 0.97 = 0.9031, so about 90.3%. Chains multiply step error rates, which is why gates between steps matter.

quiz.question: Which case best justifies moving from a workflow to an agent?
options: Requests are few and well defined
The next action depends on what each lookup returns, and the paths cannot be listed in advance
The team wants lower latency
Auditors need a fixed procedure
quiz.explanation: Agents earn their cost when the path depends on observations nobody can predict. Fixed procedures, low latency and audit needs favour workflows.

quiz.question: A payments company splits a dispute summary into three independent sections (transaction facts, customer history, policy) and runs them in parallel. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: Latency is set by the slowest section
Total tokens stay roughly the same as running them one after another
Parallel sections must share one model call
Sectioning is a form of voting
quiz.explanation: Sectioning cuts latency to the slowest part while doing the same work, so tokens are similar. Each section is its own call, and voting is a different parallel pattern.

quiz.question: A router sends 55% of requests to path A (accuracy 96%), 30% to path B (92%) and 15% to a general path (80%). What is the overall accuracy?
